addedLines: - claude: Catch-all for any task that doesn't fit a more specific agent. FleetView's default when no agent name is typed. (Tools: *)

- claude-code-guide: Use this agent when the user asks questions ("Can Claude...", "Does Claude...", "How do I...") about: (1) Claude Code (the CLI tool) - features, hooks, slash commands, MCP servers, settings, IDE integrations, keyboard shortcuts; (2) Claude Agent SDK - building custom agents; (3) Claude API (formerly Anthropic API) - Messages API for directly passing messages to Claude, Tool Runner (`client.beta.messages.tool_runner`) for running an agentic loop over your own tools, manual tool-use loops, Managed Agents for server-hosted agents with a managed sandbox, prompt caching, and general Anthropic SDK usage; (4) Claude Tag (Claude in Slack) - what it is, setting it up for a Slack workspace, `/install-slack-app`. **IMPORTANT:** Before spawning a new agent, check if there is already a running or recently completed claude-code-guide agent that you can continue via SendMessage. (Tools: Bash, Read, WebFetch, WebSearch)

- Explore: Read-only search agent for broad fan-out searches — when answering means sweeping many files, directories, or naming conventions and you only need the conclusion, not the file dumps. It reads excerpts rather than whole files, so it locates code; it doesn't review or audit it. Specify search breadth: "medium" for moderate exploration, "very thorough" for multiple locations and naming conventions. (Tools: All tools except Agent, Artifact, ExitPlanMode, Edit, Write, NotebookEdit)

- general-purpose: General-purpose agent for researching complex questions, searching for code, and executing multi-step tasks. When you are searching for a keyword or file and are not confident that you will find the right match in the first few tries use this agent to perform the search for you. (Tools: *)

- Plan: Software architect agent for designing implementation plans. Use this when you need to plan the implementation strategy for a task. Returns step-by-step plans, identifies critical files, and considers architectural trade-offs. (Tools: All tools except Agent, Artifact, ExitPlanMode, Edit, Write, NotebookEdit)
- statusline-setup: Use this agent to configure the user's Claude Code status line setting. (Tools: Read, Edit)

Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Serves this user's live capability roster and the typed call definitions. Load it whenever the user asks for an artifact needing any such runtime behavior.

Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". 3	/** Provenance of a candidate keyword. */
4	export const CANDIDATE_SOURCES = [
5	  'keywords_for_site',
6	  'ranked_keywords',
7	  'keyword_ideas',
8	  'serp',
9	  'manual',
10	  'seed',
11	] as const;
12	export type CandidateSource = (typeof CANDIDATE_SOURCES)[number];
13	
14	/** Candidate lifecycle. Scoring/rejection reasons are added in #54. */
15	export const CANDIDATE_STATUSES = ['candidate', 'selected', 'rejected'] as const;
16	export type CandidateStatus = (typeof CANDIDATE_STATUSES)[number];
17	
18	/** Search intent, shared with the DataForSEO client's normalization. */
19	export const SEARCH_INTENTS = [
20	  'informational',
21	  'commercial',
22	  'transactional',
23	  'navigational',
24	] as const;
25	export type SearchIntent = (typeof SEARCH_INTENTS)[number];
26	
27	/** Constrained article types a classified candidate can become (#54). */
28	export const ARTICLE_TYPES = [
29	  'how_to_guide',
30	  'listicle',
31	  'comparison',
32	  'definition',
33	  'product_guide',
34	  'case_study',
35	  'other',
36	] as const;
37	export type ArticleType = (typeof ARTICLE_TYPES)[number];
38	
39	/** Why a candidate was rejected by the pipeline (#54). */
40	export const REJECTION_REASONS = [
41	  'brand_navigation',
42	  'clustered_duplicate',
43	  'difficulty_ceiling',
44	  'serp_intent',
45	  'serp_authority',
46	  'serp_locality',
47	  'serp_duplicate',
48	] as const;
49	export type RejectionReason = (typeof REJECTION_REASONS)[number];
50	
51	/**
52	 * One organic SERP competitor captured during SERP validation (#144). Legacy
53	 * docs stored bare domains, so rank/url/title are null for pre-#144 entries.
54	 */
55	export const SerpCompetitorSchema = z.object({
56	  rank: z.number().int().nullable().default(null),
57	  url: z.string().nullable().default(null),
58	  domain: z.string(),
59	  title: z.string().nullable().default(null),
60	});
61	export type SerpCompetitor = z.infer<typeof SerpCompetitorSchema>;
62	
63	/** Tolerates legacy domain-only values by lifting each into a domain-only entry. */
64	export const SerpCompetitorsField = z
65	  .array(
66	    z.union([
67	      SerpCompetitorSchema,
68	      z
69	        .string()
70	        .transform((domain): SerpCompetitor => ({ rank: null, url: null, domain, title: null })),
71	    ]),
72	  )
73	  .nullable()
74	  .default(null);
75	
76	/** Canonical dedup key: lowercased, trimmed, whitespace-collapsed. */
77	export function normalizeKeyword(raw: string): string {
78	  return raw.trim().toLowerCase().replace(/\s+/g, ' ');
79	}
80	
81	/**
82	 * Candidate keyword — an org-scoped opportunity in the candidate pool, distinct
83	 * from the scheduled `keywords`/planner collection. Scoring fields
84	 * (`relevance_score`, `opportunity_score`) are populated later by #54.
85	 * See docs/superpowers/specs/2026-07-07-dataforseo-candidate-pool-design.md.
86	 */
87	export const CandidateSchema = z.object({
88	  id: z.string(),
89	  org_id: z.string(),
90	  keyword: z.string(),
91	  // Derived from `keyword` by the repository; unique per org.
92	  normalized_keyword: z.string(),
93	  source: z.enum(CANDIDATE_SOURCES),
94	  source_context: z.string().nullable().default(null),
95	  search_volume: z.number().int().nullable().default(null),
96	  difficulty: z.number().int().nullable().default(null),
97	  cpc: z.number().nullable().default(null),
98	  competition: z.number().nullable().default(null),
99	  trend: z.number().nullable().default(null),
100	  intent: z.enum(SEARCH_INTENTS).nullable().default(null),
101	  // Top-K organic results captured during SERP validation (#47/#144); null otherwise.
102	  serp_competitors: SerpCompetitorsField,
103	  relevance_score: z.number().nullable().default(null),
104	  opportunity_score: z.number().nullable().default(null),
105	  article_type: z.enum(ARTICLE_TYPES).nullable().default(null),
106	  rejection_reason: z.enum(REJECTION_REASONS).nullable().default(null),
107	  status: z.enum(CANDIDATE_STATUSES).default('candidate'),
108	  created_at: z.date(),
109	  updated_at: z.date(),
110	});
111	export type Candidate = z.infer<typeof CandidateSchema>;
112	
113	/**
114	 * Input for creating a candidate. `id`/`created_at`/`updated_at` are
115	 * server-assigned; `normalized_keyword` is derived by the repository.
116	 */
117	export const CreateCandidateInput = CandidateSchema.omit({
118	  id: true,
119	  normalized_keyword: true,
120	  created_at: true,
121	  updated_at: true,
122	});
123	// `z.input` (not `z.infer`/`z.output`) so defaulted fields (status, scores, etc.)
124	// are optional in the type, matching the runtime contract: callers pass only
125	// org_id/keyword/source and the schema fills in the rest on `.parse()`.
126	export type CreateCandidateInput = z.input<typeof CreateCandidateInput>;

20	/**

22	 * `id` is a string (the stringified Mongo `_id`); the raw `_id` never
23	 * leaves the repository layer. See design/data-layer.md.
24	 */
25	export const OrgSchema = z.object({
26	  id: z.string(),
27	  user_id: z.string(),
28	  website_url: z.string().url(),
29	  setup_status: z.enum(SETUP_STATUSES),
30	  // Billing entitlement. Defaults keep orgs stored before #56 backward-compatible.
31	  plan: z.enum(ENTITLEMENT_PLANS).default('free'),
32	  // Automatic-strategy job lifecycle (#47).
33	  strategy_status: z.enum(STRATEGY_STATUSES).default('none'),
34	  name: z.string().optional(),
35	  wordpress_token: z.string().optional(),
36	  wordpress_connected_at: z.date().optional(),
37	  // Populated by the scanner worker once scanning completes.
38	  presets: SetupPresetsSchema.optional(),
39	  // Latest 0–100 Domain Rating for the dashboard badge (#12); refreshed by the
40	  // scanner worker and the stale-refresh path in GET /dashboard/domain-rating.
41	  domain_rating: z
42	    .object({ value: z.number().int().min(0).max(100), checked_at: z.date() })
43	    .optional(),
44	  // Onboarding metadata captured at finalize (#73). Distinct from the connected
45	  // integrations concept (dashboard.integrations.connected).
46	  onboarding: z
47	    .object({
48	      referral_source: z.string().optional(),
49	      integrations: z.array(z.enum(ONBOARDING_INTEGRATIONS)).optional(),
50	    })
51	    .optional(),
52	  created_at: z.date(),
53	});
54	export type Org = z.infer<typeof OrgSchema>;
55	
56	/**
57	 * Input for creating an org — the server assigns `id` and `created_at`, and the
58	 * WordPress connection fields are server-owned (written only by
59	 * `saveWordPressConnection` after a successful integration test).

Known gaps from a keyword-pipeline audit — [#122](https://github.com/seopotion/seo/issues/122)
51:- 🟡 Keyword pipeline wired behind a paid-entitlement seam (`Org.plan`/`isPaid`): manual research API `POST /keywords/research` + `/keywords/candidates` ([#50](https://github.com/seopotion/seo/issues/50)) and an automatic 30-day content strategy — paid `/setup/finalize` → SQS strategy queue → strategy worker Lambda runs `@shared/keywords` and cluster-spreads a 30-day planner ([#47](https://github.com/seopotion/seo/issues/47)); library from [#49](https://github.com/seopotion/seo/issues/49)/[#54](https://github.com/seopotion/seo/issues/54). Deployed-env provider secret provisioning still manual/deferred ([#9](https://github.com/seopotion/seo/issues/9)/[#43](https://github.com/seopotion/seo/issues/43))
52:- ✅ Article generation (#55) — daily EventBridge scheduler fans out due planner entries to an SQS generation worker (`@shared/generation`: outline → article → humanize → deterministic + LLM validation), persists a `generated` article, and atomically links `keyword.article_id`. Cover + inline images [#51](https://github.com/seopotion/seo/issues/51): image SQS task after generation → plan → fal.ai → per-stage S3+CloudFront, idempotent per-slot retries. Images are WebP straight from fal (`output_format`, no local encoder) at a 1200px cap, stored immutable-cached, with the provider's intrinsic dimensions persisted onto each slot and published into the static-site manifest/frontmatter — [#178](https://github.com/seopotion/seo/issues/178)/[#176](https://github.com/seopotion/seo/issues/176). Articles imaged before that keep their PNGs and null dimensions (accepted). Internal links point only at the org's own published pages, derived from `presets.blog.main_blog_url` + the published slug and HTTP-verified before generation; unapproved or over-ceiling links are unwrapped and `validate.ts` rejects survivors — [#186](https://github.com/seopotion/seo/issues/186). Pre-#186 articles are cleaned with `npm run cli -- db clean-links --org <id> --apply`
54:- ✅ Dashboard UI surfaces — planner/history/settings, persisted article editor (`GET`/`PATCH /dashboard/articles/{id}` — [#74](https://github.com/seopotion/seo/issues/74)), WordPress integration, and candidate-pool UI all landed — frontend epic [#19](https://github.com/seopotion/seo/issues/19) closed. Remaining: strategy job state (pending/completed/failed) not rendered in the planner — [#65](https://github.com/seopotion/seo/issues/65)
59:- ✅ Product UI: onboarding wizard, product guard, planner/history/settings, persisted article editor + WordPress/static-site publishing, and candidate-pool UI all landed — [#20](https://github.com/seopotion/seo/issues/20)/[#19](https://github.com/seopotion/seo/issues/19) both closed. i18n routing added (next-intl, `en`/`tr`) across marketing + product. Remaining gaps: newer onboarding/article-settings prefs not fully wired to the backend — [#121](https://github.com/seopotion/seo/issues/121); no multi-org switcher — [#127](https://github.com/seopotion/seo/issues/127)
69:- ✅ Phase 0 — separate admin Lambda/HTTP API, allowlist-gated Google login + admin JWT, append-only `admin_actions` audit, org search/detail (redacted), plan override with strategy kick, `getAdminApiClient` — [#150](https://github.com/seopotion/seo/issues/150)
70:- ✅ Phase 1 — content-curation MVP: research (extracted core), candidate pool + planner curation, generate-now, article editor + WordPress publish/update, presets PATCH, strategy run, audit read — [#150](https://github.com/seopotion/seo/issues/150)
71:- ✅ Phase 2 — unstick levers: generation reset (over-cap), candidate restore, brief edit, strategy force-rerun, guarded scan re-run, image replay, WordPress connect/disconnect, GSC disconnect — [#150](https://github.com/seopotion/seo/issues/150). Backend epic complete; Phase 3 deliberately unbuilt
72:- ✅ Operator UI (`apps/admin`) — **the whole admin API is now reachable from the panel**. Vite + React SPA on the admin typed client: Google login, token-guarded shell, URL-derived stage banner, org search → workspace (tabbed) → Overview (set-plan, presets editor over the deep-merge PATCH, strategy run), candidate pool (research → add → schedule/reject), planner (reschedule/unschedule/generate-now), articles → editor (save + WordPress publish/update, images-pending guard), and the read-only Audit tab (paginated, expandable payload/`before`). Phase-2 unstick levers landed on those same screens: candidate restore, generation reset + brief edit, strategy force-rerun, scan re-run (disabled for live orgs), WordPress connect-on-behalf/disconnect, GSC disconnect, image replay. Every mutation is behind the shared two-step confirm, and a lever the API would refuse renders disabled with its reason — [#151](https://github.com/seopotion/seo/issues/151)

## Summary

Two confirmed gaps found during a keyword-research API/UI audit of the Content Planner. Both are scoped precisely below so they can be picked up independently.

---

## 1. No way to delete/reject a candidate from the keyword pool

### Problem

There is no API or UI path to remove a keyword from the candidate pool ("main keyword list"). A user can research keywords and add them to the pool, but once a keyword is in the pool there is no way to get rid of it if it's irrelevant, wrong, or a mistake.

This is **not** the same as unscheduling. `DELETE /keywords/scheduled/{keyword_id}` (`apps/api/src/routes/keywords.ts:364-408`) already exists, but it only removes a *scheduled* planner entry and returns its linked candidate back to the pool (`CandidateRepo.releaseAfterUnschedule`) — it does not delete anything from the pool itself.

### Current state (evidence)

- `CandidateSchema.status` already models a `'rejected'` value: `packages/shared/schemas/src/candidate.ts:15` (`CANDIDATE_STATUSES = ['candidate', 'selected', 'rejected']`).
- `CandidateRepo.setStatus(id, status)` already exists to flip that status: `packages/shared/db/src/repositories/candidate.repo.ts:124-130`.
- **Neither is ever called from a route.** `grep -rn "setStatus" apps/api` returns nothing — it's dead code today, only used internally by the automated scoring pipeline setting `'rejected'` on `WorkingCandidate` objects in-memory (`packages/shared/keywords/src/filters.ts`, `serp.ts`, `cluster.ts`) before they're ever persisted. There is no user-triggered path to this status.
- `GET /keywords/candidates` (`apps/api/src/routes/keywords.ts:207-242`) defaults its `status` query param to `'candidate'` (`apps/api/src/schemas/keywords.ts:60`), so a candidate set to `'rejected'` would naturally disappear from the default pool view without needing a hard delete.
- Frontend: `TargetKeywordsSection.tsx` and `ChooseKeywordModal.tsx` render candidate rows with no delete/reject action anywhere.

### Required API

Add a route to remove a candidate from the pool. Recommended shape (soft-delete via existing status enum, not a hard Mongo delete — preserves `normalized_keyword` dedup history so the same keyword isn't silently re-addable/re-researched into a duplicate):

```
DELETE /api/v0/keywords/candidates/{candidate_id}
```

- **Auth:** `authMiddleware`, ownership resolved the same way as the existing `DELETE /scheduled/{keyword_id}` handler — load the candidate by id, then `loadOwnedOrg(candidate.org_id, userId)`; 404 if either the candidate or the owning org doesn't resolve (never leak existence across accounts).
- **Paid gate:** gate on `isPaid(org)` (402 `not_paid`) for consistency with the other pool-mutation endpoint (`POST /keywords/candidates` is paid-gated via `loadOwnedPaidOrg`); `GET /keywords/candidates` is deliberately the only *unpaid* read.
- **Guard:** only a candidate currently in `status: 'candidate'` may be rejected — a `'selected'` (i.e. scheduled) candidate must be unscheduled first via the existing `DELETE /keywords/scheduled/{keyword_id}` flow. Implement as a conditional update (mirror `CandidateRepo.claimForScheduling`'s `findOneAndUpdate({ _id, status: 'candidate' }, { $set: { status: 'rejected' } })` pattern) so concurrent requests can't race past the guard.
- **Responses:**
  - `204` — candidate rejected.
  - `401` — missing/invalid bearer token.
  - `402` — org not paid.
  - `404` — candidate/org not found or not owned by caller.
  - `409` — candidate is not in `'candidate'` status (already `'selected'` or `'rejected'`) — mirror the `generation_started` 409 pattern used by `DELETE /scheduled/{keyword_id}`.
- Wire this through `CandidateRepo` (add a conditional `reject(id)` method next to `claimForScheduling`/`releaseAfterUnschedule`, following the same `findOneAndUpdate` guard style — do not just call the existing unconditional `setStatus`, since that has no race protection) and register the new route + OpenAPI schema + response types in `apps/api/src/schemas/keywords.ts` so it flows through `AppType` to the typed client.

### Frontend

- Add a delete/reject action (icon button, e.g. trash icon) per row in `TargetKeywordsSection.tsx` for candidate-sourced rows (`source: 'candidate'`), and/or in `ChooseKeywordModal.tsx`'s candidate list.
- On success, invalidate `dashboardQueryKeys.candidatePool(organizationId)` the same way `ResearchKeywordsModal.tsx`'s `handleAdd` and `ChooseKeywordModal.tsx`'s `handleSchedule` already do.
- Follow the existing error-mapping pattern (`getCandidateAddApiError`/`getCandidateScheduleError` in `planner-utils.ts`) to add a `getCandidateDeleteApiError` for the new endpoint's status codes.

### Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `DELETE /api/v0/keywords/candidates/{candidate_id}` exists, is typed through `AppType`, and is documented in the OpenAPI spec.
- [ ] Only `status: 'candidate'` rows can be rejected; scheduled (`'selected'`) candidates return `409` and must be unscheduled first.
- [ ] Rejected candidates disappear from `GET /keywords/candidates?status=candidate` (the default pool view) but are not hard-deleted.
- [ ] Ownership/ownership-leak checks match the existing `DELETE /scheduled/{keyword_id}` handler's pattern (404 for both "not found" and "not owned").
- [ ] Concurrent delete requests can't race past the status guard (unit/integration test, mirroring existing `claimForScheduling` concurrency tests).
- [ ] Frontend exposes a delete action in the pool UI, wired to the new endpoint, with loading/error states and query invalidation.
- [ ] Unit + MongoDB integration tests cover: happy path, already-scheduled conflict, not-found/not-owned, unpaid org.

---

## 2. `strategy_status: 'failed'` is silently swallowed in the UI

### Problem

The automatic 30-day content-strategy job exposes its state via `GET /dashboard/planner` → `strategy_status: 'none' | 'pending' | 'completed' | 'failed'` (`apps/api/src/schemas/dashboard.ts:120`). The frontend only special-cases `'pending'`. When the job actually **fails** (hits the DLQ after retries), the UI falls through to the normal calendar render, which looks exactly like an empty planner — no error message, no indication anything went wrong, no retry/support affordance.

content.text:
I've read the full path. Here's what actually happens, end to end.

## 0. Trigger

Four entry points all enqueue the same `StrategyTask { org_id }` onto the strategy SQS queue:

- [setup.ts:208](apps/api/src/routes/setup.ts#L208) — `/setup/finalize` for a **paid** org (`claimStrategy` makes it exactly-once)
- [apply-event.ts:55](apps/api/src/lib/billing/apply-event.ts#L55) — billing webhook upgrades org to paid
- [orgs.ts:162](apps/api/src/admin/routes/orgs.ts#L162) / [:299](apps/api/src/admin/routes/orgs.ts#L299) — admin set-plan / force-rerun
- [db.ts:123](apps/cli/src/lib/db.ts#L123) — CLI `db set-plan`

The strategy worker Lambda ([strategy.ts:146](apps/worker/src/strategy.ts#L146)) consumes it.

## 1. Worker preamble — [strategy.ts:53](apps/worker/src/strategy.ts#L53)

Loads the org, bails if no `presets` or already `completed`. Builds DataForSEO + OpenRouter clients. Reads already-scheduled keywords from `KeywordRepo` to pass as `existingKeywords`. Then calls `runKeywordPipeline`, wrapped in a deadline race that aborts 20s before the Lambda ceiling.

**The single most important input here is `org.presets`** — produced earlier by the scanner worker ([scanner.ts:57](apps/worker/src/scanner.ts#L57)), which strips the homepage HTML to **at most 8,000 chars** ([scrape.ts:2](apps/worker/src/scrape.ts#L2)) and asks the LLM for `business.{name,language,country,description}` + `audience.target[]`. Every LLM judgment downstream sees only a 5-line summary of that ([llm-prompts.ts:6](packages/shared/keywords/src/llm-prompts.ts#L6)).

## 2. The pipeline — [pipeline.ts:50](packages/shared/keywords/src/pipeline.ts#L50)

Twelve stages, all in-process:

| # | Stage | What it does |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | **gather** ([gather.ts](packages/shared/keywords/src/gather.ts)) | 3 DataForSEO Labs pulls: `keywords_for_site(own domain, limit 200)`, `ranked_keywords(each competitor, limit 200)`, then an LLM call for 10–20 seed topics (fed the top 30 competitor keywords by volume) → `keyword_ideas(seeds, limit 200)` |
| 2 | **dedupe** ([normalize.ts:36](packages/shared/keywords/src/normalize.ts#L36)) | One row per `normalizeKeyword()` (lowercase/trim/collapse); the row with most non-null metric fields wins |
| 3 | **brand/nav** ([filters.ts:47](packages/shared/keywords/src/filters.ts#L47)) | Drops keywords containing a brand token (org name words ≥3 chars + domain label) or one of 15 hardcoded English nav phrases (`login`, `pricing`, `faq`…) |
| 4 | **cluster** ([cluster.ts:35](packages/shared/keywords/src/cluster.ts#L35)) | Greedy token-Jaccard ≥ 0.6 (15 English stopwords removed); highest-volume member survives, rest → `clustered_duplicate` |
| 5 | **fill difficulty** ([filters.ts:73](packages/shared/keywords/src/filters.ts#L73)) | One `bulk_keyword_difficulty` call for every candidate still missing KD |
| 6 | **ceiling** | Drop `difficulty > 45`. Null difficulty **survives** |
| 7 | **relevance** ([score.ts:8](packages/shared/keywords/src/score.ts#L8)) | **One LLM call containing every surviving keyword**, returns `{keyword, relevance 0..1}[]` |
| 8 | **score** ([score.ts:23](packages/shared/keywords/src/score.ts#L23)) | `opportunity_score = 100 × (0.35·relevance + 0.30·log10(vol)/log10(10k) + 0.20·ease + 0.10·trend + 0.05·¬cannibal)` |
| 9 | **rank + split** | Sort by score desc; **top 40** go on, rest kept as `belowN` (unvalidated, unclassified) |
| 10 | **SERP validate** ([serp.ts:57](packages/shared/keywords/src/serp.ts#L57)) | Live Google SERP (depth 20) for each of the 40, 6-at-a-time. Reject if ≥50% of top-10 are authority domains (`wikipedia/amazon/reddit/youtube/quora/linkedin/pinterest`), or top-10 URL-set Jaccard ≥0.6 with an already-accepted keyword, then an LLM call per keyword judging `intentSuitable` / `localitySuitable` |
| 11 | **classify** ([classify.ts](packages/shared/keywords/src/classify.ts)) | One LLM call assigning `article_type` from 7 enum values to all survivors |
| 12 | **assemble** | `[accepted, belowN, rejected]` + a `stats` object |

## 3. Persist + schedule — back in [strategy.ts:80](apps/worker/src/strategy.ts#L80)

`addCandidates` inserts everything into the candidate pool (deduped against already-scheduled keywords). Then it filters for schedulable rows — `rejection_reason === null && search_volume !== null && difficulty !== null && not already scheduled` — sorts by `opportunity_score`, and takes the top 30.

`clusterSpreadSchedule` ([schedule.ts:14](packages/shared/keywords/src/schedule.ts#L14)) round-robins those 30 by `article_type` so adjacent days differ, stamps one per day, and `scheduleCandidate` writes each to `KeywordRepo` (skipping to the next free date on collision). Org → `strategy_status: 'completed'`.

---

## Where quality leaks

Ranked by how much I think each contributes to what you're seeing:

**1. Nothing in the pipeline ever judges the keyword *string*.** DataForSEO returns real search queries — typos, mobile fragments, ungrammatical phrasings, foreign-language mixes. The only string-level gates are the 15-phrase English nav blacklist and token-Jaccard clustering. A malformed keyword that has volume and low KD sails straight through to becoming an article title. This is almost certainly your "grammatically weird" complaint.

**2. Relevance scoring — 0.35 of the score — probably collapses silently.** [score.ts:14](packages/shared/keywords/src/score.ts#L14) sends *all* survivors (plausibly 400–1000) in one prompt with **no `maxTokens`**, and [parseRelevance](packages/shared/keywords/src/llm-prompts.ts#L66) requires an **exact string match** on the returned keyword. Anything truncated, dropped, re-cased or trimmed by the model gets `relevance = 0` with no error. When that happens the ranking degenerates to "high volume + low difficulty" — which is exactly how generic junk floats to the top. Same exact-match fragility in `parseClassification` (falls back to `'other'`, which then defeats the day-spreading logic).

**3. No volume floor, and no filtering pushed to the API.** `SiteKeywordsParams` only carries target/location/language/limit — no `order_by`, no `filters`. So you get an arbitrary 200-row slice per endpoint, not the best 200. And `search_volume: 0` is schedulable (only `!== null` is checked).

**4. Candidates ranked 41+ can get scheduled without ever being SERP-validated.** `belowN` keeps `rejection_reason: null`, so if SERP rejects more than 10 of the top 40, the worker's `selectable` filter silently backfills from unvalidated, unclassified (`article_type: null`) candidates.

**5. SERP judgment fails open.** [parseSerpJudgment](packages/shared/keywords/src/llm-prompts.ts#L117) returns `{intentSuitable: true, localitySuitable: true}` on any unparseable response — LLM hiccups *admit* bad keywords rather than reject them.

**6. You're flying blind.** `runKeywordPipeline` computes a full `stats` object (gathered, afterDedupe, afterBrandNav, afterCeiling, accepted, `rejectedByReason`) and [strategy.ts:80](apps/worker/src/strategy.ts#L80) **throws it away**. Nothing is logged, so today you can't tell which stage is doing the damage.

**7. Clustering and stopwords are English-only.** Token Jaccard on a 15-word English stopword list. For a Turkish or other agglutinative-language org, near-duplicates won't cluster — you get 30 near-identical topics.

**8. `existingArticleKeywords` is hardcoded `[]`** ([strategy.ts:67](apps/worker/src/strategy.ts#L67)) with a stale comment referencing #55, which has since landed. Cannibalization against already-written articles never fires.

---

My recommendation for the next step: **before changing anything, make the pipeline observable.** Log the `stats` object and dump the actual per-stage survivors for one real org, so we can see empirically whether relevance is collapsing (finding 2) and where the volume goes. Guessing at weights without that is how this gets worse.

Two things that would help me target this:

1. Can you paste ~10 real bad keywords from a recent run, and tell me the org's language/country? That tells me instantly whether this is the string-quality problem (#1) or the ranking-collapse problem (#2).
2. Do you have access to a staging org I can run the pipeline against, or should I build the instrumentation to be run by you?

Those four examples are diagnostic. Let me show you the arithmetic, because it names the root cause precisely.

## Why "water bath canner" beat your real keywords

Plug it into [score.ts:29](packages/shared/keywords/src/score.ts#L29):

```
volume  = log10(22201) / log10(10000) = 4.35/4 = 1.087 → clamped to 1.00
ease    = 1 − (0/100)                                  = 1.00
trend   = null → 0.50
cannibal= 0    → 1.00
raw = 0.35·r + 0.30(1.00) + 0.20(1.00) + 0.10(0.50) + 0.05(1.00)
    = 0.35·r + 0.60
```

**A keyword with zero relevance to your business has a score floor of 60.** Volume ≥10k saturates the volume term at max, and KD 0 saturates ease at max. Junk gets 0.50 of the score for free.

Now a real Clewas keyword — say "reverse osmosis membrane fouling", volume ~480, KD ~30, relevance 0.95:

```
raw = 0.35(0.95) + 0.30(0.671) + 0.20(0.70) + 0.10(0.5) + 0.05(1) = 0.774 → 77
```

77 beats 60. **So relevance is probably working fine** — my earlier hypothesis #2 was likely wrong for your case. The real problem is different:

## The actual root cause: a hard quota with no quality floor

`REJECTION_REASONS` ([candidate.ts:40](packages/shared/schemas/src/candidate.ts#L40)) is `brand_navigation, clustered_duplicate, difficulty_ceiling, serp_intent, serp_authority, serp_locality, serp_duplicate`.

**There is no relevance-based rejection.** `applyRelevance` writes a score that feeds ranking and then *nothing ever vetoes on it*. Combined with `PLAN_DAYS = 30` and `.slice(0, budget)` in [strategy.ts:106](apps/worker/src/strategy.ts#L106), the pipeline is **obligated** to produce 30 entries. Clewas is a niche B2B — its addressable keyword universe is maybe 15–25 genuinely relevant terms. Slots 20–30 get padded from the score-60 junk tier. The pipeline scrapes the barrel by construction.

Three contributing faults behind that:

**1. The seed prompt asks for exactly the wrong thing.** [llm-prompts.ts:37](packages/shared/keywords/src/llm-prompts.ts#L37) says *"Return 10-20 short, **generic** topic seeds."* For Clewas that yields seeds like "water treatment", "water purification", "desalination". Those go into `keyword_ideas` ([gather.ts:56](packages/shared/keywords/src/gather.ts#L56)) — DataForSEO's **category-expansion** endpoint, which returns everything in the same topical bucket. That's how a home canning pot ends up in a desalination SaaS content plan. `keyword_suggestions` (long-tail phrases *containing* the seed) would be far safer for a B2B niche; `keyword_ideas` is a consumer-SEO tool.

**2. KD 0 is treated as "maximum ease" when it's really "no data."** All four of your examples have difficulty 0. DataForSEO returns 0/null for keywords it lacks KD data on, and [score.ts:33](packages/shared/keywords/src/score.ts#L33) converts that into the best possible ease score. **A missing-data signal is being rewarded as an ideal one.**

**3. The scoring model encodes consumer-SEO assumptions.** More volume = better, monotonically, saturating at 10k. For niche B2B, a 22,200-volume keyword is *evidence you're in the wrong market*. You want a volume band (say 50–3,000), not a ceiling.

Also note "aqual water" and "aquan water" both at volume 14,800 — identical volume means DataForSEO is bucketing typo variants of one brand term. And they **don't cluster**: tokens `{aqual, water}` vs `{aquan, water}` → Jaccard 1/3 = 0.33, under the 0.6 threshold. Both survive as "distinct" topics. Lexical clustering can't see they're the same thing.

One thing I can't determine without logs: "water bath canner" should have been killed at stage 10 (its SERP is product/commercial → `intentSuitable: false`). Either the LLM judgment failed open, or it was never SERP-validated at all because it came from the `belowN` backfill. That's exactly why instrumentation comes first.

---

## On topic clusters: do it second, but decide two things now

Short answer: **it doesn't break anything, and you should not fold it into this task — but it's not merely "later" either, because it's the correct fix for the quota problem.**

Here's the tension, stated honestly. Your instinct is right that clusters are part of the quality answer: **5 well-chosen clusters × 6 articles = 30 articles from 5 genuinely relevant topics**, instead of needing 30 independently-relevant keywords that Clewas doesn't have. That directly dissolves the padding problem I described above. So it's not orthogonal.

But sequencing still matters: clustering a polluted pool gives you *well-organized garbage*. "aqual water" + "aquan water" + "spring v purified water" would form a lovely cluster. Input quality is strictly upstream of cluster quality.

**My recommendation — two phases:**

**Phase 1 (this task):** observability, gather/seed fixes, KD-0 handling, volume band, and a **relevance floor that rejects rather than ranks**. Critically: *let the plan under-fill*. If only 18 keywords clear the bar, schedule 18. Today's silent padding to 30 is the bug; producing fewer, better entries is correct behavior, and Phase 2 is what legitimately refills the calendar.

**Phase 2:** the cluster system — pillar/support roles, cluster-aware selection and scheduling, cluster context in generation, and internal links (#186) that finally point somewhere meaningful.

**Two decisions to make now, in Phase 1, so Phase 2 isn't a rewrite:**

1. **Stop discarding cluster membership.** [cluster.ts:51](packages/shared/keywords/src/cluster.ts#L51) currently *rejects* members as `clustered_duplicate` — it throws away exactly the data the cluster system needs. Change it to *record* `cluster_id` on the candidate even though nothing consumes it yet. Cheap now, expensive to reconstruct later.
2. **Don't over-invest in the flat top-30 selection** in [strategy.ts:93-110](apps/worker/src/strategy.ts#L93-L110) — Phase 2 replaces it wholesale. Fix the filters, leave the selection shape alone.

---

Before I write a plan, one decision from you:

Phase 1 has a cheap-and-certain part (relevance floor, KD-0 handling, volume band, logging the `stats` that's currently discarded) and a more invasive part (replacing `keyword_ideas` with `keyword_suggestions`, rewriting the seed prompt to be niche-specific, pushing `filters`/`order_by` down to DataForSEO). The second part costs real API credits to validate.

Do you want me to **(a)** start with instrumentation only — log the per-stage funnel and dump one real Clewas run so we can see exactly where those four keywords entered and why SERP validation didn't kill them, then decide the fixes from evidence; or **(b)** go straight to implementing the full Phase 1 on the diagnosis above?

I'd recommend (a) — it's one small PR, and it settles the `belowN`-backfill-vs-LLM-failed-open question that changes which fix matters most.

The reason 1.1 comes first: `addCandidates` persists **every** candidate including rejected ones, with `relevance_score`, `opportunity_score`, `rejection_reason`, `source`, and `serp_competitors` intact. Your last Clewas run is fully reconstructable from the database.

The single sharpest test: **`serp_competitors === null` on a scheduled keyword means it was never SERP-validated** — it was backfilled from the `belowN` tier. That one field settles the question I couldn't answer.

`--snapshot` is just **an output file path you make up**. The command runs the pipeline live, and writes everything the providers returned into that file. Later, `--replay <same path>` re-runs the pipeline reading from that file instead of calling the network. You're not typing a snapshot — you're naming a file for it to create.

Here's the full sequence.

## Step 0 — Save the untracked work first

You're on `dev` and both tools are untracked. One stray `git clean` loses them.

```bash
cd /Users/alperyazagan/Repos/seo
git checkout -b Alperadoss/strategy-diagnostics
git add apps/cli
git commit -m "[cli] strategy-audit + strategy-dryrun diagnostics

Part of #NNN"
```

Do this before anything else. Land the PR later (Step 6) — you don't need it merged to run the tool.

## Step 1 — Preconditions

Mongo running:

```bash
docker compose up -d mongo
```

Root `.env` (not `apps/cli/.env` — `npm run cli` loads `.env` from the repo root) needs:

```
MONGO_URI=mongodb://localhost:27017
DATAFORSEO_LOGIN=...
DATAFORSEO_PASSWORD=...
OPENROUTER_API_KEY=...
```

⚠️ **Gotcha:** make sure `MONGO_URI_PARAM`, `DATAFORSEO_LOGIN_PARAM`, `DATAFORSEO_PASSWORD_PARAM` and `OPENROUTER_API_KEY_PARAM` are **commented out or absent**. If any `*_PARAM` is set, the resolver goes to AWS SSM instead of reading the plain env var, and you'll get a confusing credentials error.

Keep snapshots out of git:

```bash
mkdir -p .snapshots
echo ".snapshots/" >> .gitignore
```

## Step 2 — Cheap smoke test first

Don't spend the full run until you know the plumbing works. `--serp-top-n 3` makes this ~3 SERP calls instead of 40:

**My relevance-floor leverage prediction was wrong.** I said cutting the 188 zeros would free SERP slots and push `accepted` "well above 15." It went 15→18. **And the `serp_intent` data overturns my framing of the whole problem.**

## The judge isn't broken — it's telling us something worse

`reverse osmosis system` (rel 1.0), `reverse osmosis membrane` (rel 1.0), `reverse osmosis industrial` (rel 1.0) — all rejected on intent. My instinct was that this meant the prompt was misfiring on good keywords.

It isn't. **The judge is correct.** Its prompt asks "could a blog article we write rank here?" and the US SERP for `reverse osmosis system` is Home Depot, Culligan, Waterdrop, Amazon. Google has decided that query means *"I want to buy a home RO unit."* A Clewas blog post cannot rank there. Rejecting it is the right call.

Which means the actual finding is this:

> **Clewas's head terms are owned by consumer ecommerce. Every high-volume keyword that is genuinely about their business is structurally unwinnable.** The winnable B2B intent lives in low-volume, technical, problem-framed queries — membrane fouling prevention, antiscalant dosing, SWRO energy recovery, permeate flux decline.

And the pipeline is systematically biased *against exactly those*:

- `volumeCap: 10_000` with monotonic log scoring rewards volume all the way up, so head terms always outrank the 30–200/mo technical queries that Clewas can actually win
- `keywords_for_site` and `keyword_ideas` at `limit: 200` with no `order_by` and no `filters` return an arbitrary slice — and `gathered: 400` being exactly 200+200 proves we truncated data the provider was willing to give
- the seed prompt literally asks for *"generic"* topic seeds, which is the wrong instruction for a niche B2B
- there's no mechanism anywhere that seeks long-tail technical phrasing

**The most valuable thing in that reject list is `evoqua reverse osmosis` and `evoqua ro system` at relevance 0.8.** Evoqua is a real industrial water-treatment vendor, and it surfaced *organically* despite `presets.audience.competitors` being empty and the `ranked_keywords` branch of `gather.ts` being completely disabled. That's proof the competitor keyword space is rich and entirely untapped — one of three gather sources has never run for this org.

There's also a neat idea hiding in the rejects: a relevance-1.0 keyword killed on intent means the *topic* is right and the *modifier* is wrong. `reverse osmosis system` fails, but "how industrial reverse osmosis systems handle fouling" wouldn't. Those 9 clearly-relevant rejects are ideal seeds for a long-tail expansion pass rather than dead weight.

## What this means for the roadmap

The 17-entry result isn't a shortfall to paper over — it's the honest measure of how many winnable standalone keywords exist for this business. 1.3b should raise it, but not to 30. **Phase 2's cluster system is now clearly load-bearing, not a nice-to-have:** a handful of validated pillars expanded into supporting long-tail articles is the only legitimate way to fill a 30-day calendar for a niche B2B.

Same failure was hiding in the SERP judge: 2 of 139 judgments were also empty bodies, fail-opened to intentSuitable: true.

article_type: before → after
100% other (78/78) → spread. Latest live run (60 accepts): definition 36, how_to_guide 7, other 7, listicle 4, case_study 3, product_guide 2, comparison 1. The plan itself now spans 5 types, so clusterSpreadSchedule has something to work with.

serpJudge   sent 118  judged 118  UNPARSEABLE 0  batches 12  dead 0
classify    sent 60   typed 60  rows 60  matched 60  validType 60  batches 3  dead 0
Timing — full live runs
before	live #1	live #2
total	693s (79%)	240.1s (27.3%)	341.0s (38.8%)
SERP fetch+judge	~630s	83.7 + 47.1	66.1 + 46.6
relevance	~60s all-stages	78.9s	197.5s
Target of ≤7 min met with room. Batch size 10, judge concurrency 8, fetch concurrency 12 — sized from the recorded prompts (~537 prompt tokens/keyword, so batch-10 lands near 4k) and the measured fact that a judge call costs ~30s whether it covers 1 keyword or 10, so trips were the cost, not tokens.

Three things you need to know
1. Batching amplified the empty-body failure, and I had to fix it. The first batched live run showed UNPARSEABLE 20, dead 2 — 20 of 150 keywords accepted unjudged versus 2 of 139 before. Concentrating 10 keywords per call concentrates the blast radius. I added a single retry on an empty completion in the OpenRouter client; the next run measured 0 unparseable. This does not change the fail-open policy — if the retry also comes back empty, the empty result is returned and the existing path runs unchanged.

2. serp_intent moved 57 → 55 on the replay, and I verified it is not misalignment. 15 individual verdicts flipped (net +3 accepts). I pulled the recorded batch bodies and checked every reason against its own keyword — all coherent (wastewater trade shows → "event listing and trade show directory pages"; chemical dosing systems → "mostly product pages"). Adjacent near-duplicates now agree with each other, which they did not always do before. So: model variance on borderline keywords under a reworded prompt, not index scrambling.

But one reason read "Similar to the singular version, results are mostly product pages" — the model is referring to another keyword in the batch. Batching introduces cross-keyword context that per-keyword judging did not have, despite the prompt saying to judge each independently. Here it made near-duplicates more consistent, but it is a genuine semantic difference and you should know it exists.

3. Cross-run pool comparison is noisy. gathered was 870 / 1257 / 982 across three runs because the seed LLM is non-deterministic and the seeds drive the whole keyword_suggestions fan-out. Don't read accept-count deltas between live runs as signal.

What I'd look at next (not done — out of scope)
Relevance is now the largest single stage and the widest variance (78.9s vs 197.5s), and it is still one call for 409 keywords — structurally the same shape that broke classify. It has the coverage counters to detect a failure but no batching to contain one. That's the next timeout and correctness risk, and it's a separate change.

Finding (d) is the single most important thing this whole investigation has turned up, and it's bigger than the classifier.

## The model is silently returning nothing

```
completionTokens: 65536, text: ""
```

GLM-5.2 spent its entire output ceiling on reasoning tokens and emitted zero content. `tryParse('')` → null → every keyword kept its seed value. Cost $0.159 to produce nothing, and **failed completely silently** because all three parse helpers in `llm-prompts.ts` are written to degrade quietly rather than throw.

My casing hypothesis was wrong, and more to the point it was the wrong *kind* of hypothesis — I was looking for a parsing bug when the problem was that no response existed to parse. Good instinct going to the recorded response first instead of implementing the fix I'd specified.

This is not a classify bug. It's a property of running a reasoning model on structured extraction tasks with no reasoning budget control, and it affects **every LLM call in the pipeline** — seeds, relevance, SERP judgment, classification. You already saw it hit 2/139 judgments before batching and 20/150 after.

**And there's a failure mode you should know about right now, in production code:**

`parseRelevance` seeds every keyword to 0. The relevance floor we added rejects everything at exactly 0. So if the relevance call returns empty — the same failure that just hit classify, on a call that sends 409 keywords in one shot — **every candidate gets rejected, and the job produces an empty 30-day plan.** The floor converted a silent-degradation failure into a total-failure one. Your implementer's closing note flagged relevance as the next risk; it's sharper than that, because the floor is already merged.

The retry-on-empty in the OpenRouter client is a good stopgap, but one retry against a systemic behavior isn't a fix. The real levers are reasoning-budget control (OpenRouter exposes reasoning-control parameters — verify the exact shape against their current docs rather than guessing) or simply not using a reasoning model for these tasks. Seeds, relevance scoring, intent judgment and classification are cheap structured extraction; they don't need frontier reasoning, and a non-reasoning model would be faster, cheaper and immune to this.

## Timing: solved, with room

693s → 240s/341s, 79% → 27–39% of budget. Target met. The insight behind it is the good part — *"a judge call costs ~30s whether it covers 1 keyword or 10, so trips were the cost, not tokens"* — that's measurement driving the design rather than intuition.

## Your three notes

**Batching amplifying the empty-body failure (20 unparseable vs 2)** — correctly identified and correctly fixed in scope. Worth stating plainly: batching didn't cause that bug, it made an existing one 10× more visible. That's an argument for batching, not against it.

**The cross-keyword contamination is real and I'd accept it, with one caveat.** *"Similar to the singular version, results are mostly product pages"* is the model reasoning across batch members despite instructions. You're right that it made near-duplicates more consistent. The caveat: **batch composition depends on ranking order, which depends on scores** — so any future scoring change reshuffles batches and can flip verdicts for reasons unrelated to the change being tested. That weakens the replay fixture as a stable baseline. Not a reason to revert; a reason to expect noise when you diff.

**Cross-run pool variance is the one that worries me most operationally.** `gathered` at 870 / 1257 / 982 across three runs, driven by a non-deterministic seed LLM at `temperature: 0`, means **you currently cannot A/B test a pipeline change.** A ±40% swing in pool size swamps the effect of anything you'd want to measure. Before Phase 2 — where you'll be comparing cluster strategies — you need a way to pin seeds for benchmark runs so the fan-out is reproducible. Otherwise every future "before → after" is unfalsifiable.

Minor, non-blocking: `definition` at 36 of 60 looks skewed — `ro membrane cleaning procedure pdf` and `how to install ro membrane` should be `how_to_guide`. The classifier works now; it may just be lazy. Worth a glance during Phase 2 when `article_type` starts driving cluster roles.

## Where this leaves us

You've gone from a plan of 30 junk keywords to 30 on-topic ones, with the job at 27–39% of budget instead of 79%. The remaining work splits cleanly:

**1.3d — hardening (small, and I'd do it before Phase 2).** Batch relevance the way judge and classify now are; get reasoning under control or move these four calls off a reasoning model; make an empty-response failure loud instead of silent — specifically, refuse to produce a plan when relevance coverage is poor rather than rejecting the entire pool; and pin seeds for reproducible benchmark runs.

**Phase 2 — clusters.** Still the main event, and the thing that makes those six near-duplicate membrane-cleaning keywords into one pillar with five supports instead of six articles competing with each other.

# Building LLM-Powered Applications with Claude

This skill helps you build LLM-powered applications with Claude. Choose the right surface based on your needs, detect the project language, then read the relevant language-specific documentation.

## Before You Start

Scan the target file (or, if no target file, the prompt and project) for non-Anthropic provider markers — `import openai`, `from openai`, `langchain_openai`, `OpenAI(`, `gpt-4`, `gpt-5`, file names like `agent-openai.py` or `*-generic.py`, or any explicit instruction to keep the code provider-neutral. If you find any, stop and tell the user that this skill produces Claude/Anthropic SDK code; ask whether they want to switch the file to Claude or want a non-Claude implementation. Do not edit a non-Anthropic file with Anthropic SDK calls. (Exception: the `prompt-audit` subcommand is non-interactive and does not stop here — it records non-Anthropic provider markers in its report's stated assumptions and never proposes switching a non-Anthropic file to the Anthropic SDK.)

## Output Requirement

When the user asks you to add, modify, or implement a Claude feature, your code must call Claude through one of:

1. **The official Anthropic SDK** for the project's language (`anthropic`, `@anthropic-ai/sdk`, `com.anthropic.*`, etc.). This is the default whenever a supported SDK exists for the project.
2. **Raw HTTP** (`curl`, `requests`, `fetch`, `httpx`, etc.) — only when the user explicitly asks for cURL/REST/raw HTTP, the project is a shell/cURL project, or the language has no official SDK.

Never mix the two — don't reach for `requests`/`fetch` in a Python or TypeScript project just because it feels lighter. Never fall back to OpenAI-compatible shims.

**Never guess SDK usage.** Function names, class names, namespaces, method signatures, and import paths must come from explicit documentation — either the `{lang}/` files in this skill or the official SDK repositories or documentation links listed in `shared/live-sources.md`. If the binding you need is not explicitly documented in the skill files, WebFetch the relevant SDK repo from `shared/live-sources.md` before writing code. Do not infer Ruby/Java/Go/PHP/C# APIs from cURL shapes or from another language's SDK.

**If WebFetch or repository access fails** (network restricted, timeouts, clone blocked): do not keep retrying — write code from the patterns and namespace/package tables in the `{lang}/` file, run the compiler or interpreter on it, and iterate on the error output. For statically-typed SDKs (C#, Java, Go) a compile-fix loop against local errors reaches working code faster than blocked network research.

## Defaults

Unless the user requests otherwise:

For the Claude model version, please use Claude Opus 5, which you can access via the exact model string `claude-opus-5`. Please default to using adaptive thinking (`thinking: {type: "adaptive"}`) for anything remotely complicated. And finally, please default to streaming for any request that may involve long input, long output, or high `max_tokens` — it prevents hitting request timeouts. Use the SDK's `.get_final_message()` / `.finalMessage()` helper to get the complete response if you don't need to handle individual stream events

## ⚠️ API Drift — Your Training Prior May Be Stale

Several common Claude API shapes changed in 2025–2026. If you recall a pattern from training, verify it against the `{lang}/` files in this skill before writing — the rows below are the most frequent drift points:

| Area | Stale prior | Current API |
|---|---|---|
| Extended thinking | `thinking: {type: "enabled", budget_tokens: N}` | On Claude 4.6+ models: `thinking: {type: "adaptive"}`. `budget_tokens` is deprecated on Opus 4.6 / Sonnet 4.6 and **rejected with a 400** on Fable 5 / Sonnet 5 / Opus 5 / 4.8 / 4.7. Pre-4.6 models still use `budget_tokens`. |
| Web search / web fetch tool type | `web_search_20250305`, `web_fetch_20250910` | `web_search_20260209`, `web_fetch_20260209` (dynamic filtering) on Opus 5/4.8/4.7/4.6, Sonnet 5, and Sonnet 4.6. Older models keep the basic variants; on Vertex AI only basic `web_search_20250305` is available (web fetch is not on Vertex) — see the Server Tools QR below. |
| PHP parameter names | snake_case wire names as named args (`max_tokens`) | Top-level named args are camelCase (`maxTokens`). Nested array keys vary by feature (e.g. `'taskBudget'`, `'skillID'`, `'mcp_server_name'`) — copy the exact key from the documented example; do not bulk-convert. |
| Managed Agents credentials | Keep secrets host-side via custom tools (the only option before vaults shipped) | Vault `environment_variable` credentials — stored by Anthropic, substituted at egress, never visible in the sandbox (`shared/managed-agents-tools.md` → Vaults). Host-side custom tools remain the fallback for self-hosted sandboxes. |

The `{lang}/` files in this skill are authoritative over recalled patterns.

---

## Subcommands

If the User Request at the bottom of this prompt is a bare subcommand string (no prose), search every **Subcommands** table in this document — including any in sections appended below — and follow the matching Action column directly. This lets users invoke specific flows via `/claude-api <subcommand>`. If no table in the document matches, treat the request as normal prose.

Do not summarize the guide — execute it. If the user did not name a target model, ask which model to migrate to in the same turn as the scope question. After the per-target changes are applied, audit the in-scope prompt text, tool descriptions, and request code against `shared/prompt-audit.md` — prompting written for the source model is part of every migration, and it does not announce itself. |

## Language Detection

Before reading code examples, determine which language the user is working in (exception: for the `prompt-audit` subcommand, skip this section's ask steps — the audit is non-interactive and its inventory is language-agnostic; when no language is inferable, proceed without asking and state the assumption in the report):

   - `*.rb`, `Gemfile` → **Ruby** — read from `ruby/`
   - `*.cs`, `*.csproj` → **C#** — read from `csharp/`

2. **If multiple languages detected** (e.g., both Python and TypeScript files):

   - If still ambiguous, ask: "I detected both Python and TypeScript files. Which language are you using for the Claude API integration?"

3. **If language can't be inferred** (empty project, no source files, or unsupported language):

   - Use AskUserQuestion with options: Python, TypeScript, Java, Go, Ruby, cURL/raw HTTP, C#, PHP
   - If AskUserQuestion is unavailable, default to Python examples and note: "Showing Python examples. Let me know if you need a different language."

4. **If unsupported language detected** (Rust, Swift, C++, Elixir, etc.):

   - Suggest cURL/raw HTTP examples from `curl/` and note that community SDKs may exist
   - Offer to show Python or TypeScript examples as reference implementations

5. **If user needs cURL/raw HTTP examples**, read from `curl/`.

### Language-Specific Feature Support

Every SDK language above supports both the beta Tool Runner and Managed Agents (beta) — Python (`@beta_tool` decorator), TypeScript (`betaZodTool` + Zod), Java (annotated classes), Go (`BetaToolRunner` in the `toolrunner` pkg), Ruby (`BaseTool` + `tool_runner`), C# (`BetaToolRunner` + raw JSON schema), PHP (`BetaRunnableTool` + `toolRunner()`); code entry points are in the Tool Use Patterns quick reference below. cURL is raw HTTP (no SDK features) and supports Managed Agents.

> **Managed Agents code examples**: see the reading guide in the `## Managed Agents (Beta)` section below.

---

## Which Surface Should I Use?

> **Start simple.** Default to the simplest tier that meets your needs. Single API calls and workflows handle most use cases — only reach for agents when the task genuinely requires open-ended, model-driven exploration. "Simplest" means the least code you own: for a hosted, scheduled, or memory-backed agent, Managed Agents is usually the simplest option (no loop code, no state files, no scheduler), even though it's a bigger platform.

| Use Case                                        | Tier            | Recommended Surface       | Why                                                          |
| ----------------------------------------------- | --------------- | ------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------ |
| Classification, summarization, extraction, Q&A  | Single LLM call | **Claude API**            | One request, one response                                    |
| Batch processing or embeddings                  | Single LLM call | **Claude API**            | Specialized endpoints                                        |
| Multi-step pipelines with code-controlled logic | Workflow        | **Claude API + tool use** | You orchestrate the loop                                     |
| Custom agent with your own tools                | Agent           | **Claude API + tool use** | Maximum flexibility                                          |
| Server-managed stateful agent with workspace    | Agent           | **Managed Agents**        | Anthropic runs the loop and hosts the tool-execution sandbox |
| Persisted, versioned agent configs              | Agent           | **Managed Agents**        | Agents are stored objects; sessions pin to a version         |
| Long-running multi-turn agent with file mounts  | Agent           | **Managed Agents**        | Per-session containers, SSE event stream, Skills + MCP       |
| Agent that runs on a schedule (cron, "every night") | Agent       | **Managed Agents** — scheduled deployments | Deployments fire sessions autonomously; no client-side scheduler |

> **Note:** Managed Agents is the right choice when you want Anthropic to run the agent loop *and* host the container where tools execute — file ops, bash, code execution all run in the per-session workspace. If you want to host the compute yourself or run your own custom tool runtime, Claude API + tool use is the right choice — use the tool runner for the agentic loop — its per-turn hooks still give you approval gates, logging, error interception, and conditional execution (see `shared/tool-use-concepts.md`) — or the manual loop when you want to own the entire loop yourself.

> **Cloud-provider access.** **Claude Platform on AWS** is Anthropic-operated with same-day API parity — see `shared/claude-platform-on-aws.md` for client setup. For per-feature availability on **Claude Platform on AWS**, **Amazon Bedrock**, **Google Vertex AI**, and **Microsoft Foundry**, see `shared/platform-availability.md` — that table is the single source of truth in this skill; do not infer availability from anywhere else.

### Building an Agent: Four Approaches

Once you've decided you actually need an agent (open-ended, model-driven tool use), there are four distinct ways to build one. Two independent questions separate them: **who supplies the harness** (the agent loop + context management) and **who supplies the deployment** (the infra the agent runs on). The Tool Runner and the Claude Agent SDK both supply a *harness only* — you still host and deploy them yourself — which is why they're easy to conflate. Managed Agents (CMA) is the only option that supplies **both** the harness *and* managed deployment; the manual loop supplies neither.

| # | Approach | You write | Harness & deployment | Tools available | Use when |
|---|----------|-----------|----------------------|-----------------|----------|
| 1 | **Claude API — manual loop** | The `while stop_reason == "tool_use"` loop yourself | You build the harness; you host | Only tools you define | You want to own the *entire* loop — no beta dependency, or a control flow the Tool Runner's per-turn hooks don't fit |
| 2 | **Claude API — Tool Runner** (`client.beta.messages.tool_runner` + `@beta_tool` / `betaZodTool`) | Just the tool functions | SDK supplies the loop (**harness only**); you host | Only tools you define | A custom-tool agent without hand-writing the loop (most cases). Per-turn hooks still give you approval gates, error interception, result modification (e.g. `cache_control`), retries, streaming, and compaction |
| 3 | **Managed Agents** (REST, beta) | Agent config + your tool results | Anthropic supplies the harness **and** hosts a per-session sandbox (**harness + deployment**) | Anthropic-hosted sandbox (bash, files, code exec) + Skills/MCP + your tools | You want Anthropic to run the loop *and* host the per-session workspace; persisted/versioned configs; long-running sessions |
| 4 | **Claude Agent SDK** — *separate product* (`claude-agent-sdk` / `@anthropic-ai/claude-agent-sdk`) | A prompt + options | SDK supplies the Claude Code harness + built-in tools (**harness only**); you host | Built-in Read/Write/Edit/Bash/Glob/Grep/WebSearch/WebFetch + MCP + subagents | You want a batteries-included coding/filesystem agent running on your own infra |

The harness/deployment split is the key mental model: options 1, 2, and 4 all **leave deployment to you**; only option 3 (CMA) adds managed deployment. Options 1–3 are what this skill generates; option 4 is a different library with its own docs — see the disambiguation below.

> **Tool Runner ≠ Claude Agent SDK.** These sound alike but are different packages:
> - **Tool Runner** is part of the regular Anthropic API SDK (`anthropic` / `@anthropic-ai/sdk`), reached via `client.beta.messages.tool_runner`. It automates the request → execute → loop cycle *for tools you define*. No built-in tools, no filesystem access, no sandbox — you supply every tool and host the compute. It is option 2 above, a thin helper over `POST /v1/messages`.
> - **Claude Agent SDK** (`claude-agent-sdk` / `@anthropic-ai/claude-agent-sdk`) is Claude Code packaged as a library. It ships built-in tools (file read/write/edit, bash, grep, web search), the full agent loop, context management, hooks, subagents, permissions, and sessions. You call `query(prompt, options)` and it drives everything.
>
> Both are **harness-only — you host and deploy them.** The difference is scope of harness: the Tool Runner loops over tools *you* define (with per-turn hooks for approval, interception, result modification, and retries — but no built-in tools); the Agent SDK is the full Claude Code harness with built-in tools. Neither provides managed deployment — that's what **Managed Agents (CMA)** adds (Anthropic hosts the loop and a per-session sandbox).
>
> **This skill covers the Claude API and Managed Agents (options 1–3); it does not generate Claude Agent SDK code.** If the user actually wants the Claude Agent SDK, point them to its docs (`code.claude.com/docs/en/agent-sdk`) — don't substitute the API Tool Runner for it, or vice-versa.

### Should I Build an Agent?

Before choosing the agent tier, check all four criteria:

- **Complexity** — Is the task multi-step and hard to fully specify in advance? (e.g., "turn this design doc into a PR" vs. "extract the title from this PDF")
- **Value** — Does the outcome justify higher cost and latency?
- **Viability** — Is Claude capable at this task type?
- **Cost of error** — Can errors be caught and recovered from? (tests, review, rollback)

If the answer is "no" to any of these, stay at a simpler tier (single call or workflow).

## Architecture

Everything goes through `POST /v1/messages`. Tools and output constraints are features of this single endpoint — not separate APIs.

**User-defined tools** — You define tools (via decorators, Zod schemas, or raw JSON), and the SDK's tool runner handles calling the API, executing your functions, and looping until Claude is done. For full control, you can write the loop manually.

**Server-side tools** — Anthropic-hosted tools that run on Anthropic's infrastructure. Code execution is fully server-side (declare it in `tools`, Claude runs code automatically). Computer use can be server-hosted or self-hosted.

**Structured outputs** — Constrains the Messages API response format (`output_config.format`) and/or tool parameter validation (`strict: true`). The recommended approach is `client.messages.parse()` which validates responses against your schema automatically. Note: the old `output_format` parameter is deprecated; use `output_config: {format: {...}}` on `messages.create()`.

**Supporting endpoints** — Batches (`POST /v1/messages/batches`), Files (`POST /v1/files`), Token Counting (`POST /v1/messages/count_tokens` — see `shared/token-counting.md`), and Models (`GET /v1/models`, `GET /v1/models/{id}` — live capability/context-window discovery) feed into or support Messages API requests.

### Claude Fable 5 (`claude-fable-5`) — most capable widely released model

Claude Fable 5 is Anthropic's most capable widely released model, for the most demanding reasoning and long-horizon agentic work; everything below also applies to **Claude Mythos 5** (`claude-mythos-5`, Project Glasswing — same capabilities, pricing, and API surface; successor to the invitation-only `claude-mythos-preview`). 1M context window (the maximum is also the default), 128K max output. Key API differences from Opus-tier — see `shared/model-migration.md` → Migrating to Claude Fable 5 for details:

- **Thinking is always on** — omit the `thinking` parameter entirely (or send `{type: "adaptive"}`). Any other explicit configuration is rejected: `{type: "disabled"}` and `{type: "enabled", budget_tokens: N}` both return a 400. Control depth with `output_config.effort` (supports `low` through `xhigh` and `max`).
- **The raw chain of thought is never returned** — responses carry regular `thinking` blocks (not `redacted_thinking`): `display: "summarized"` returns a readable summary, `"omitted"` (the default) leaves the `thinking` field as an empty string. Replay rules: pass thinking blocks back unchanged on the same model; other models drop them silently (unbilled — nothing to strip); details in `shared/model-migration.md`.
- **Tokenizer** — same tokenizer as Opus 4.8 (introduced with Opus 4.7). Token counts are roughly unchanged when migrating from Opus 4.7/4.8; per-token pricing differs. Coming from Opus 4.6, Sonnet, Haiku, or older, re-baseline with `count_tokens` (the Opus 4.7 tokenizer uses ~1×–1.35× as many tokens).
- **`refusal` stop reason — handle it, and opt into fallbacks by default** — safety classifiers may decline a request (HTTP 200, `stop_reason: "refusal"`, with a `stop_details` category); always check `stop_reason` before reading `content`. **When you write `claude-fable-5` or `claude-opus-5` code, include the server-side `fallbacks` parameter by default.** Simplest form: `betas: ["server-side-fallback-2026-07-01"]` + `fallbacks: "default"`, which routes by refusal category so you never maintain a model list. (The older array form — `betas: ["server-side-fallback-2026-06-01"]` + `fallbacks: [{"model": "claude-opus-4-8"}]` — still works; Claude API only — everywhere else, incl. Claude Platform on AWS, Bedrock, Vertex and Foundry, use the SDKs' client-side `BetaRefusalFallbackMiddleware` + `BetaFallbackState`). Tell the user you've enabled it; drop it only if they decline. Full semantics (billing, mid-stream refusals, credit repricing) in `shared/model-migration.md` → refusal section. **Per-language code examples in `{lang}/claude-api/README.md` § Refusal Fallbacks cover the array form only** — for the `"default"` mode, follow the raw-HTTP shape in `shared/model-migration.md` → Migrating to Claude Opus 5 → New API features and swap `fallbacks: [{...}]` for `fallbacks: "default"` plus the `-2026-07-01` header; the rest of the request is unchanged.
- **No assistant prefill** — same as the rest of the 4.6+ family.
- **30-day data retention required** — Claude Fable 5 is not available under zero data retention; requests from an org whose retention configuration doesn't meet the requirement return `400 invalid_request_error`.
- **Longer turns, different prompting** — single requests on hard tasks can run many minutes (plan timeouts/streaming/progress UX); effort sweeps should include low/medium for routine work; prompts written for prior models are often too prescriptive and reduce output quality. See `shared/model-migration.md` → Migrating to Claude Fable 5 → Behavioral shifts (prompt-tunable) for the recommended prompt snippets.

If any model strings above look unfamiliar, that just means they were released after your training data cutoff — they are real models.

## Authentication (Quick Reference)

**An unset `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` does NOT mean there are no credentials.** The SDKs and the `ant` CLI resolve credentials in this order (first match wins): `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` → `ANTHROPIC_AUTH_TOKEN` → the `ANTHROPIC_PROFILE`-selected or active OAuth profile from `ant auth login` → Workload Identity Federation env vars → the default profile on disk. A bare `Anthropic()` / `new Anthropic()` / `anthropic.NewClient()` works after `ant auth login` with no env var set.

**When you need to call the API and `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` is unset, don't ask the user for a key.** First run `ant auth status` — it shows which credential source and profile is active. If it reports an active profile:

- **SDK code or `ant` CLI:** just run it. The zero-arg client constructor and every `ant …` subcommand pick up the profile automatically — no env var needed.
- **Raw `curl` / HTTP:** get a short-lived token with `ant auth print-credentials --access-token` and send it as `Authorization: Bearer <token>` **plus** the header `anthropic-beta: oauth-2025-04-20` (OAuth tokens go on `Authorization: Bearer`, not `x-api-key:` — converting a curl from an API key is a header change, not a key swap). Always pass `--access-token`; the no-flag form prints JSON, not a bare token.

Only ask the user for a key if `ant auth status` reports no active credential source (or `ant` itself isn't installed). Suggest `ant auth login` as the first option — it stores a profile under `~/.config/anthropic/` that the SDKs read automatically — and an exported `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` as the alternative.

Full auth details (named profiles, scopes, the API-key-shadows-profile trap, refresh-token expiry): `shared/anthropic-cli.md`.

## Thinking & Effort (Quick Reference)

Use adaptive thinking (`thinking: {type: "adaptive"}`) on every current model — Claude dynamically decides when and how much to think. Per-model rules:

| Model | Thinking config | Omitting `thinking` | `budget_tokens` | Sampling (`temperature`/`top_p`/`top_k`) | Effort levels |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Fable 5 | `{type: "adaptive"}` or omit; explicit `{type: "disabled"}` returns 400 — omit the param instead | Runs adaptive (thinking is always on) | Removed — `{type: "enabled", budget_tokens: N}` returns 400 | Removed — 400 | `low`/`medium`/`high`/`xhigh`/`max` |
| Claude Opus 5 | `{type: "adaptive"}` or omit; `{type: "disabled"}` accepted **only at effort `high` or below** — 400 at `xhigh`/`max`, and see the disabled-thinking pitfall below | Runs **adaptive** (thinking is on by default — unlike Opus 4.8/4.7) | Removed — 400 | Removed — 400 | `low`–`max` (all five) |
| Opus 4.8 / 4.7 | `{type: "adaptive"}` is the only on-mode; `{type: "disabled"}` accepted | Runs **without** thinking — set `{type: "adaptive"}` explicitly | Removed — 400 | Removed — 400 | `low`/`medium`/`high`/`xhigh`/`max` |
| Sonnet 5 | `{type: "adaptive"}` is the only on-mode; `{type: "disabled"}` accepted | Runs adaptive | Removed — 400 | Removed — 400 | `low`/`medium`/`high`/`xhigh`/`max` |
| Opus 4.6 / Sonnet 4.6 | `{type: "adaptive"}` (recommended; auto-enables interleaved thinking, no beta header) | Set `{type: "adaptive"}` explicitly | Deprecated — do not use in new code; transitional escape hatch only (see below) | Allowed | `low`/`medium`/`high`/`max` (`xhigh` arrived with Opus 4.7) |
| Older (Sonnet 4.5, Haiku 4.5, …) — only if explicitly requested | `{type: "enabled", budget_tokens: N}` | No thinking | Required for thinking; must be less than `max_tokens`, minimum 1024 — errors otherwise | Allowed | `effort` works on Opus 4.5 (`low`/`medium`/`high` only — no `xhigh`/`max`); errors on Sonnet 4.5 / Haiku 4.5 |

Opus 4.8 keeps the same request surface as 4.7 (no new breaking changes) — see `shared/model-migration.md` → Migrating to Opus 4.8 for the behavioral re-tuning, and → Migrating to Opus 4.7 for the full breaking-change list when coming from 4.6 or earlier. With `thinking` disabled, Opus 4.8 may write longer reasoning into the visible response — leave adaptive thinking on, or add a final-answer-only instruction (see the migration guide).

- **Effort (GA, no beta header):** `output_config: {effort: "low"|"medium"|"high"|"xhigh"|"max"}` — inside `output_config`, not top-level; default `high` (equivalent to omitting it). Controls thinking depth and overall token spend; combine with adaptive thinking for the best cost-quality tradeoffs. `xhigh` (added on Opus 4.7, between `high` and `max`) is the best setting for most coding and agentic use cases on Fable 5 / Opus 4.7/4.8 / Sonnet 5, and the default in Claude Code; effort matters more on those models than on any prior model in their tier — re-tune it when migrating, and run long-horizon/agentic tasks at `high`/`xhigh` with the full task spec given up front. Use a minimum of `high` for intelligence-sensitive work, `max` when correctness matters more than cost, and `low` for subagents or simple tasks — lower effort means fewer and more-consolidated tool calls, less preamble, and terser confirmations (`high` is often the sweet spot balancing quality and token efficiency).
- **Thinking display — `"omitted"` by default on Fable 5 / Mythos 5 / Opus 5 / 4.8 / 4.7 / Sonnet 5:** `display: "summarized"` returns a readable summary of the reasoning; `"omitted"` (the default on all six — a silent change from Opus 4.6 and Sonnet 4.6, where it was `"summarized"`) streams `thinking` blocks with empty text. `display` controls visibility only — thinking happens and is billed the same under every setting; the raw chain of thought is never exposed on any model. If you stream reasoning to users, the default looks like a long pause before output — set `thinking: {type: "adaptive", display: "summarized"}` explicitly. (Independent of display, echo thinking blocks back unchanged when continuing on the same model; other models silently ignore them — see the migration guide.)
- **When the user asks for "extended thinking", a "thinking budget", or `budget_tokens`:** always use Fable 5, Opus 5, 4.8, 4.7, or 4.6 with `thinking: {type: "adaptive"}` — the fixed thinking-token-budget concept is deprecated and adaptive thinking replaces it. Do NOT use `budget_tokens` for new 4.6/4.7/4.8 code and do NOT switch to an older model just because the user mentions it. *Gradual-migration carve-out:* `budget_tokens` is still functional on Opus 4.6 and Sonnet 4.6 only, as a transitional escape hatch for existing code that needs a hard token ceiling before you've tuned `effort` — see `shared/model-migration.md` → Transitional escape hatch. It is fully removed on Fable 5, Opus 5/4.7/4.8, and Sonnet 5.

## Compaction (Quick Reference)

**Beta, Fable 5, Opus 5, Opus 4.8, Opus 4.7, Opus 4.6, Sonnet 5, and Sonnet 4.6.** For long-running conversations that may exceed the 1M context window, enable server-side compaction. The API automatically summarizes earlier context when it approaches the trigger threshold (default: 150K tokens). Requires beta header `compact-2026-01-12`.

**Critical:** Append `response.content` (not just the text) back to your messages on every turn. Compaction blocks in the response must be preserved — the API uses them to replace the compacted history on the next request. Extracting only the text string and appending that will silently lose the compaction state.

See `{lang}/claude-api/README.md` (Compaction section) for code examples. Full docs via WebFetch in `shared/live-sources.md`.

## Prompt Caching (Quick Reference)

**Prefix match.** Any byte change anywhere in the prefix invalidates everything after it. Render order is `tools` → `system` → `messages`. Keep stable content first (frozen system prompt, deterministic tool list), put volatile content (timestamps, per-request IDs, varying questions) after the last `cache_control` breakpoint.

**Mid-conversation operator instructions** (Claude Opus 5, Claude Opus 4.8, Claude Fable 5, Claude Mythos 5; not Claude Sonnet 5; no beta header): append `{"role": "system", ...}` to `messages[]` instead of editing top-level `system`. Preserves the cached history prefix and is the prompt-injection-safe operator channel. See `shared/prompt-caching.md` § Mid-conversation system messages.

**Top-level auto-caching** (`cache_control: {type: "ephemeral"}` on `messages.create()`) is the simplest option when you don't need fine-grained placement. Max 4 breakpoints per request. Minimum cacheable prefix is ~1024 tokens — shorter prefixes silently won't cache.

**Verify with `usage.cache_read_input_tokens`** — if it's zero across repeated requests, a silent invalidator is at work (`datetime.now()` in system prompt, unsorted JSON, varying tool set).

For placement patterns, architectural guidance, and the silent-invalidator audit checklist: read `shared/prompt-caching.md`. Language-specific syntax: `{lang}/claude-api/README.md` (Prompt Caching section).
